options.misconception: The table shows the opposite: incumbents lost in 1980 and 1992.
options.text: Voters consistently rewarded the party in power with larger majorities in every election.

options.misconception: No third-party candidate won an electoral vote in these years.
options.text: Third-party candidates regularly won electoral votes and decided the outcome of elections.

options.misconception: Democrats won in 1992 and 1996, so Republicans did not win every contest in the period.
options.text: Republican candidates won every presidential election between 1980 and 2000.
Landslide victories gave way to narrow, closely divided elections as the period went on.

rationales.A: The table shows the opposite: incumbents lost in 1980 and 1992. Background: Carter lost in 1980 and the elder Bush lost in 1992, so voters did not consistently reward the party in power.
rationales.B: No third-party candidate won an electoral vote in these years. Background: Perot won nearly a fifth of the popular vote in 1992 but no electoral votes at all.
rationales.C: Democrats won in 1992 and 1996. Background: Clinton carried both elections, so Republicans did not win every contest in the period.
rationales.D:
The table shows the pattern: 525 electoral votes in 1984, then 426, 370, 379, and finally 271 in 2000, when the winner lost the popular vote. Background: the 2000 election was decided by the Supreme Court in Bush v. Gore after a disputed Florida recount.
Wide margins at the start of the period, knife-edge margins at the end — that is a country growing more evenly and bitterly divided.
rationales.general:
1. Read the columns, not the names. Electoral votes fall from 525 to 271 across the table.
2. Watch the popular vote too. Reagan won by 18 points in 1984; in 2000 the winner trailed his opponent.
3. Ask what the pattern means. Background: the 2000 election ended in the Supreme Court, a sign of how evenly the country had split.
4. Rule out the easy stories. Incumbents lost, third parties won no electors, and both parties won elections.
Remember: the table tells the story of the period in one line — big wins first, a dead heat last.

source: original; stimulus table drawn from the American Presidency Project election data, via the Gilder Lehrman Institute
stem: Which conclusion about American politics in this period is best supported by the table?

stimulus.source_note: Data from the American Presidency Project, via the Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History.
stimulus.text:
Presidential election results, 1980–2000:

| Year | Winner | Winner's popular vote | Runner-up's popular vote | Winner's electoral votes |
| 1980 | Ronald Reagan (R) | 50.7% | Carter 41.0% | 489 |
| 1984 | Ronald Reagan (R) | 58.8% | Mondale 40.6% | 525 |
| 1988 | George H. W. Bush (R) | 53.4% | Dukakis 45.6% | 426 |
| 1992 | Bill Clinton (D) | 43.0% | Bush 37.4% | 370 |
| 1996 | Bill Clinton (D) | 49.2% | Dole 40.7% | 379 |
| 2000 | George W. Bush (R) | 47.9% | Gore 48.4% | 271 |

Ross Perot, running as an independent, won 18.9% of the popular vote in 1992 and 8.4% in 1996, winning no electoral votes in either year.
